claims.text: Conventional PVD produces an elemental Cr coating with a relatively random grain structure and numerous high-diffusivity grain boundaries.
Adjusting substrate bias, deposition temperature, and deposition rate can produce a dense, columnar, low-defect Cr coating.
A PVD deposition-temperature range of 200–400°C is suitable for engineering the proposed coating microstructure.
The engineered columnar microstructure will have less grain-boundary area than the conventional coating.
Reducing grain-boundary area lowers the number of fast diffusion paths available for Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Grain boundaries are the primary channels for rapid atomic diffusion in the coated Cr–Zr system.
Reducing grain-boundary density will limit diffusion of Cr into the Zr-alloy substrate during transient high-temperature exposure.
Limiting Cr diffusion into the substrate will preserve coating integrity during high-temperature transients.
The tailored coating will have a significantly lower rate of interdiffusion-induced degradation than the conventional Cr coating during transient steam exposure near 1200°C.
The tailored coating will maintain reliable corrosion protection during continuous subcritical-water exposure near 300°C.
The defect-rich microstructure of the conventional elemental Cr coating accelerates Cr–Zr interdiffusion at high temperature.
The proposed operating boundary is subcritical water near 300°C.
The proposed accident boundary is steam exposure up to approximately 1200°C for seconds to minutes.
Effectiveness depends on producing a uniformly optimized microstructure over large coating areas.
Effectiveness also depends on retention of the engineered microstructure during repeated high-temperature transients.
